meta.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
meta.author: bank-team-web-development
meta.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.topic: What a key does for a row that carries no key of its own
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a stable row key matters during list reconciliation
questions.stem: A list renders five rows from an array; one row has no key of its own. What does React use as the key, and what can go wrong?

options.text: It uses the array index and reordering can corrupt row state
It uses null and skips rendering that row entirely
options.misconception: confuses a missing key with a null render

options.text: It uses the array index; reordering can corrupt which row holds which state
options.misconception: treats the index as a stable identity for mutable rows

options.text: It generates a UUID automatically for every unkeyed row
options.misconception: assumes React invents identifiers for missing keys

questions.explanation: React falls back to the array index when no key is supplied. Reordering or deleting then attaches state to the wrong row because the index is positional, not identity. Give each row a stable unique key.
questions.hint: Index keys break when list order changes.

questions.topic: Reading a nested document and the query it cannot serve
questions.learningObjective: Identify when a query cannot be served by a nested document shape
questions.stem: Given orders stored as {customer:{id,city}, items:[{sku,qty}]}, which query cannot be answered without reshaping?

options.text: Find orders whose any item sku equals X
options.misconception: thinks nested arrays are directly indexable by sku
ignores that customer.city is reachable in one path

options.text: Find orders with more than two items
options.misconception: assumes array length is not stored in the document

questions.explanation: Customer id is a simple nested field and is directly queryable. The challenge is multi-item predicates that need array traversal, not single nested scalars. Reshape or index accordingly.
questions.hint: Single nested scalars are queryable directly.

questions.topic: A column rename and the query it leaves behind
questions.learningObjective: Recognize stale queries after a column rename
questions.stem: A column was renamed from name to title, but a SELECT name still ships in production. What is the failure mode?

options.text: The database returns null for name silently
options.misconception: assumes a missing column yields null not an error

options.text: The ORM maps name to title by convention
The rename is rolled back automatically
options.misconception: thinks DDL renames are transactionally reversible by clients

options.text: The query fails at parse time with unknown column

questions.explanation: A renamed column makes references to the old name invalid, so the statement errors at parse or plan time. Update all queries, views, and mappings together.
questions.hint: Old column names are not aliases.

questions.topic: A backfill run in small batches and the lock it avoids holding
questions.learningObjective: Explain why backfills use small batches to limit lock duration
questions.stem: Why does a backfill that updates millions of rows run in small batches instead of one statement?

answer.exemplar: Small batches commit frequently so each lock is held briefly, letting other transactions proceed and avoiding long table locks and replication lag.

questions.explanation: One giant update holds locks and bloats the transaction log. Batching commits between chunks releases locks and keeps replication healthy. Pause between batches if needed.

questions.topic: A deleted row that a unique index still remembers
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a unique index blocks reinserting a deleted value
questions.stem: A row is deleted, yet inserting the same value into a unique column fails. Why?

options.text: The delete has not committed in this session
A concurrent transaction still holds the value
options.misconception: blames concurrency for a committed delete

options.text: The index retains tombstones until vacuum
options.misconception: confuses soft delete with index tombstones

options.text: Unique indexes cannot be reused after deletion
options.misconception: thinks uniqueness is permanent across deletions

questions.explanation: If the delete is uncommitted or visibility rules hide it, the unique constraint still sees the value. Commit the delete or check transaction state before reinserting.
questions.hint: Uncommitted deletes still occupy unique values.

questions.topic: A unique index that refuses a swap of two values
questions.learningObjective: Describe how to swap two values under a unique constraint
questions.stem: Two rows must swap unique codes A and B. A direct UPDATE fails. What is the safe sequence?

options.text: Update both rows in one statement with a CASE
options.misconception: assumes a single statement bypasses uniqueness checks

options.text: Delete both rows then reinsert swapped
options.misconception: risks losing data and foreign keys
treats index toggling as a safe production step

options.text: Move one value to a temporary unused code, then swap

questions.explanation: Use an intermediate value that satisfies uniqueness, then move both rows. This avoids constraint violations without dropping data or disabling indexes.
questions.hint: Stage through a free intermediate value.

questions.topic: A foreign key that refuses an orphan and then a parent
questions.learningObjective: Explain foreign key ordering for inserts and deletes
questions.stem: Which order avoids a foreign key violation when creating a child and its parent?

options.misconception: ignores that the child needs an existing parent

options.text: Insert both in one transaction in any order
Insert child with a null parent then update
options.misconception: works only if the column is nullable

questions.explanation: Foreign keys require the parent to exist when the child is inserted unless constraints are deferred. Insert the parent first, then the child.

questions.topic: An index and the plan it replaces
questions.learningObjective: Describe how an index changes a query plan
questions.stem: Before an index, a plan scans every row. After adding an index on status, what does the plan likely do for WHERE status='open'?

options.text: Still scans all rows because indexes are hints
Sorts the table by status first
options.misconception: treats index creation as a sort step at query time

options.text: Builds a hash table of all statuses
options.misconception: confuses a seek with a hash aggregate

options.text: Uses an index seek on status

questions.explanation: A usable index on the filtered column lets the optimizer seek directly to matching entries instead of scanning. Verify with EXPLAIN.
questions.hint: Indexes enable seeks for equality predicates.

questions.topic: A composite index and the order its columns have to be in
questions.learningObjective: Explain leftmost prefix rule for composite indexes
questions.stem: An index is on (city, age). Which query can use it efficiently without a full scan?

options.misconception: thinks column order in predicate changes index usage
assumes a trailing wildcard prefix is sargable

questions.explanation: Composite indexes are used from the left. A query on city alone or city plus age can seek; age alone cannot use the leading city. Predicate order does not matter.

questions.topic: A covering index and the table visit it removes
questions.learningObjective: Identify when an index covers a query
questions.stem: An index on (status, created_at) includes name. A query selects name, status where status='open'. What table access is avoided?
questions.explanation: When all selected columns are in the index, the engine answers from the index alone and skips the table heap lookup. This is a covering index.

questions.topic: A table scan in a plan and three ways to end it
questions.learningObjective: List ways to eliminate a sequential scan
questions.stem: A plan shows a sequential scan on a large table. Name three ways to make it use an index instead.

answer.exemplar: Add an index on the filtered column, make the predicate sargable by removing functions on the column, or reduce selectivity so the optimizer prefers an index seek.

questions.explanation: Scans happen when no index fits, the predicate is non-sargable, or most rows match. Fix the predicate or add a targeted index and recheck EXPLAIN.

questions.topic: A cursor and an offset after a row above the page is deleted
questions.learningObjective: Compare cursor and offset pagination after a deletion
questions.stem: Using OFFSET, a row above the current page is deleted. What happens to the next page?

options.text: The page shifts and one row is skipped
OFFSET automatically adjusts to the deletion
The page is unchanged because OFFSET counts rows
options.misconception: confuses counting rows with stable positions

options.text: The cursor jumps to the deleted row

questions.explanation: OFFSET is positional, so deleting a row above shifts everything and a row is skipped. Cursor pagination avoids this by anchoring on a value.

questions.topic: A cursor whose row is deleted before the next page is asked for
questions.learningObjective: Handle a cursor row that disappears before next page
questions.stem: Cursor pagination stores last_seen_id=42, but row 42 is deleted before the next request. What should the API do?

options.text: Return an empty page because 42 is gone
options.misconception: treats a missing cursor as end of data
surfaces internal state as a hard error

options.text: Resume using the value 42 as the exclusive lower bound

options.misconception: discards progress on a transient deletion

questions.explanation: The cursor value is a bound, not a required row. Query rows with id greater than 42; deletion does not invalidate the bound. This keeps pagination stable.
questions.hint: A cursor is a bound, not a row.

questions.topic: Overlapping pages and the duplicates an endless list has to drop
questions.learningObjective: Deduplicate overlapping pages in infinite scroll
questions.stem: Infinite scroll fetches pages that overlap by two rows. How should the client merge them?

options.text: Append all rows and let the UI show duplicates
Replace the whole list with the latest page
Deduplicate by row id when merging

questions.explanation: Overlaps can happen due to inserts or retries. Merge by a stable row id and keep the first occurrence to avoid duplicates in the rendered list.
questions.hint: Deduplicate by stable id on merge.

questions.topic: A rejected optimistic update and the newer edit a rollback discards
questions.learningObjective: Explain rollback behavior after a rejected optimistic update
questions.stem: An optimistic update is rejected by the server because a newer edit exists. What does rollback do?

options.text: Reverts to the last server-confirmed value
Keeps the optimistic value and retries

questions.explanation: On rejection the client discards its optimistic change and restores the last known server state. The newer server edit remains authoritative.

questions.topic: A whole row write that overwrites a field nobody meant to change
questions.learningObjective: Prefer partial updates to avoid clobbering fields
questions.stem: A PUT replaces the entire row from a stale client object, wiping a field updated by another user. What is the fix?

options.text: Send the full object more often
Add a version column and retry forever
options.misconception: treats retry as a substitute for partial writes

options.text: Lock the row for the whole session
Use PATCH with only changed fields

questions.explanation: Partial updates send only changed fields, so unrelated concurrent changes survive. Combine with version checks for safety.
questions.hint: PATCH sends deltas, not whole rows.

questions.topic: An offline queue and the retry policy that empties it
questions.learningObjective: Choose a retry policy that drains an offline queue
questions.stem: An offline queue holds failed requests. Which retry policy best empties it without hammering the server?

options.text: Retry all at once when online returns

options.misconception: never gives up and wastes battery

questions.explanation: Exponential backoff with jitter spreads retries and avoids synchronized bursts. Cap retries and persist the queue across sessions.

questions.topic: A message delivered three times and the consumer that applies it once
questions.learningObjective: Make a consumer idempotent under duplicate delivery
questions.stem: A message is delivered three times. What makes the consumer apply its effect once?

options.text: The consumer checks a processed-id set before acting

questions.explanation: Consumers must be idempotent. Track processed message ids and skip duplicates so repeated delivery has no extra effect.

questions.topic: A gap in a sequence and the messages that must wait for it
questions.learningObjective: Explain in-order delivery with sequence gaps
questions.stem: Messages 1,2,4 arrive; 3 is missing. What must the consumer do before processing 4?

options.text: Drop 4 and request resend of all

questions.explanation: Out-of-order arrival requires buffering until the missing sequence number arrives, or timing out and requesting resend. Processing 4 first violates ordering.

questions.topic: A device that missed a delete and comes back with an old edit
questions.learningObjective: Resolve stale edits from an offline device
questions.stem: A device missed a delete and later pushes an old edit. How should the server resolve it?

options.text: Apply the edit because it is newer by client clock
options.misconception: trusts a fast or stale client clock

options.text: Recreate the deleted item with the edit
Reject the edit because the item no longer exists
Merge the edit into the delete tombstone

questions.explanation: If the item is deleted, a stale edit must be rejected or ignored. Client clocks cannot override server authority on existence.

questions.topic: What a document shape permits that a table of columns cannot
questions.learningObjective: Contrast document and relational modeling
questions.stem: What can a document store do that a fixed-column table cannot?

options.misconception: confuses document stores with relational engines

options.text: Store rows with different fields per record

questions.explanation: Documents allow heterogeneous shapes per record, while relational tables require a fixed schema. Choose based on query and consistency needs.

questions.topic: The write cost an index adds
questions.learningObjective: Explain write amplification from indexes
questions.stem: Each extra index slows writes. Why does adding an index increase write cost?

answer.exemplar: Every insert or update must maintain each index, so more indexes mean more writes, more lock contention, and slower commits.

questions.explanation: Indexes are not free on writes. Each index entry must be inserted or updated, increasing IO and lock time. Add only indexes that serve real queries.
questions.hint: Each index is another write per row.

questions.topic: Reading the three words a plan uses to describe its work
questions.learningObjective: Interpret EXPLAIN output keywords
questions.stem: In a query plan, which three words indicate a full table scan?

options.misconception: confuses a seek with a scan
thinks join strategy is a scan type

questions.explanation: Seq Scan means the engine reads every row. Index Seek or Index Scan indicate index usage. Check the plan before tuning.

questions.topic: A server-sent event and the one direction it allows
questions.learningObjective: State the directionality of SSE
questions.stem: Server-Sent Events allow communication in which direction?
questions.explanation: SSE is a one-way server-to-client stream over HTTP. Use WebSockets for bidirectional traffic.

questions.topic: A socket that closes and the handshake that reopens it
questions.learningObjective: Describe WebSocket reconnect handshake
questions.stem: A WebSocket drops. What does the client do to reopen?

options.text: Send a new HTTP GET to the same URL and upgrade
Reuse the old socket object without handshake
Ping the server until it responds
options.misconception: ping does not reopen a closed socket

questions.explanation: After a close, a new connection requires a fresh HTTP upgrade handshake. The old socket cannot be revived.
questions.hint: Closed sockets need a new handshake.

questions.topic: What actually delivers an ordering guarantee
questions.learningObjective: Identify what provides message ordering
questions.stem: What actually delivers an ordering guarantee for messages?

options.misconception: confuses processing order with delivery order

options.text: A single partition or sequence number

questions.explanation: Ordering requires a single ordered channel, partition, or sequence numbers. Networks and consumers do not guarantee order by themselves.
questions.hint: Order comes from a single ordered channel.

questions.topic: A batching window and the latency it buys with
questions.learningObjective: Explain the latency tradeoff of batching
questions.stem: A batching window collects events for 50ms before sending. What latency does it buy, and what does it cost?

answer.exemplar: It reduces per-message overhead and IO by grouping, but adds up to the window length of latency to each event.

questions.explanation: Batching trades latency for throughput. Tune the window to meet latency targets while reducing request overhead.

questions.topic: A delta sync and the baseline it is measured from
questions.learningObjective: Define delta sync baseline
questions.stem: A delta sync sends only changes since the last sync. What is the baseline?

options.misconception: time is not a stable sync baseline

options.text: The client's last acknowledged version or cursor

questions.explanation: Delta sync compares against the client's last acknowledged version or cursor. Without that baseline, the server cannot know what changed.

questions.topic: How long a tombstone has to be kept
questions.learningObjective: Determine tombstone retention period
questions.stem: A tombstone must be kept longer than the longest offline client gap. If the longest gap is 7 days, how many days must it be retained at minimum?

options.misconception: equals the gap, leaving no safety margin

questions.explanation: Retention must exceed the longest offline gap so a returning client can see the deletion. Eight days covers a seven-day gap with margin.
questions.hint: Retention must exceed the longest gap.

questions.topic: A client clock four minutes fast and an empty delta set
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a fast client clock empties a delta set
questions.stem: A client clock is four minutes fast, so its since timestamp is in the future. What happens to the delta set?

options.misconception: assumes future timestamp means full history

options.text: The server errors on invalid timestamp
The server returns an empty set
The client retries with server time
options.misconception: describes recovery, not the immediate result

questions.explanation: A future since timestamp means no changes are considered newer, so the delta is empty. Sync the client clock or use server-issued cursors.

questions.topic: Choosing an invalidation strategy for a cache
questions.learningObjective: Choose a cache invalidation strategy
questions.stem: Which invalidation strategy best keeps a cache fresh without excessive origin load?

options.text: No invalidation, rely on TTL only
Invalidate on write plus short TTL fallback

questions.explanation: Write-through invalidation keeps data fresh, and a short TTL catches missed invalidations. Pure TTL risks staleness; global invalidation overloads origin.
questions.hint: Invalidate on write, TTL as fallback.

questions.topic: A subscription that is registered twice and torn down once
questions.learningObjective: Avoid duplicate subscription registration
questions.stem: A component registers a subscription twice but tears it down once. What leaks?
questions.explanation: Each registration needs a matching teardown. A missing teardown leaves a dangling subscription, causing duplicate events and leaks.

questions.topic: A polling interval chosen without counting the cost
questions.learningObjective: Account for cost when choosing a poll interval
questions.stem: A poll every 100ms seems responsive. What cost is often ignored?

options.text: Battery and network usage on clients

options.misconception: DNS is cached, not per poll

questions.explanation: Frequent polling drains battery and bandwidth on clients and load on servers. Choose intervals based on staleness tolerance and cost.

questions.topic: A long poll and the connections it holds open
questions.learningObjective: Describe long polling connection cost
questions.stem: Long polling holds connections open waiting for data. What is the main cost?

options.misconception: responses are not stored on disk

options.text: Server memory and file descriptors per idle client

questions.explanation: Each held connection consumes server resources even when idle. Scale connection limits and consider SSE or WebSockets.

questions.topic: Server authoritative state and a body the client filled in
questions.learningObjective: Enforce server authority over client-submitted state
questions.stem: A client submits a body claiming isAdmin=true. What should the server do?

options.text: Trust the body to reduce latency
options.misconception: trusts client input for privileged state

options.text: Ignore isAdmin and derive it server-side

options.misconception: wrong status for a field issue

questions.explanation: Never trust client-supplied privileged fields. Derive authorization and protected state on the server from authenticated identity.

questions.topic: A merge rule and the edit it discards when two branches diverge
questions.learningObjective: Apply a merge rule that discards a conflicting edit
questions.stem: Two branches edit the same field; the merge rule keeps the later timestamp. Which edit is discarded?

options.text: The edit with the later timestamp
The edit with the earlier timestamp

questions.explanation: A last-write-wins rule keeps the later edit and discards the earlier one. Make sure timestamps are reliable or use version vectors.

questions.topic: What a key does for a row that carries no key of its own
questions.learningObjective: Choose a stable key for a dynamic list
questions.stem: A todo list can reorder items. Which key should each item use?
questions.explanation: Use a stable unique id so React matches the same item across reorders and preserves its state.

questions.topic: Reading a nested document and the query it cannot serve
questions.learningObjective: Identify a query that needs aggregation over a nested array
questions.stem: orders has items:[{sku,qty}]. Which query needs aggregation rather than a simple path?

options.text: Find orders where any item sku is X
options.misconception: thinks any-item is a simple path

questions.explanation: Summing across a nested array requires aggregation, not a direct field path. Model and index accordingly.

questions.topic: A column rename and the query it leaves behind
questions.learningObjective: Plan a safe column rename migration
questions.stem: How do you rename a column without breaking running queries?

answer.exemplar: Add the new column, backfill, update code to read and write both, deploy, then drop the old column after traffic drains.

questions.explanation: A phased migration keeps old and new names available during rollout. Dropping too early breaks in-flight clients.

questions.topic: A backfill run in small batches and the lock it avoids holding
questions.learningObjective: Size a batch to balance throughput and lock time
questions.stem: A backfill processes 100000 rows in batches of 500. How many batches are needed?
questions.explanation: 100000 divided by 500 equals 200 batches. Smaller batches reduce lock time at the cost of more commits.

questions.topic: A deleted row that a unique index still remembers
questions.learningObjective: Handle unique constraint after deletion in a transaction
questions.stem: Inside one transaction you delete a row then insert the same unique value. Why might it still fail?

options.misconception: thinks deletion is permanent for uniqueness

options.text: The insert runs before the delete
The delete is not yet visible to the insert

questions.explanation: Within the same transaction visibility rules may still see the deleted row for uniqueness. Commit between steps or defer constraints.

questions.topic: A unique index that refuses a swap of two values
questions.learningObjective: Perform a safe swap under unique constraint
questions.stem: Swap unique codes X and Y between two rows. Which SQL approach avoids a constraint error?

options.text: UPDATE t SET code=CASE id WHEN 1 THEN 'Y' WHEN 2 THEN 'X' END
options.misconception: assumes row-level uniqueness is checked after statement

options.text: Delete both rows and insert swapped
Use a temporary placeholder code for one row first

questions.explanation: Stage one row to an unused placeholder, then move the other, then move the first. This respects uniqueness at every step.

questions.topic: A foreign key that refuses an orphan and then a parent
questions.learningObjective: Order deletes to satisfy foreign keys
questions.stem: To delete a parent and its child, what order avoids a foreign key violation?

options.text: Set child parent to null then delete parent
Delete both in any order in one transaction

questions.explanation: Remove dependents before the parent. With cascading deletes configured, the database can do this automatically.

questions.topic: An index and the plan it replaces
questions.learningObjective: Verify index usage with EXPLAIN
questions.stem: After adding an index, which plan node confirms it is used?

options.misconception: a scan means no index used

questions.explanation: Look for Index Scan or Index Seek in EXPLAIN. A remaining Seq Scan means the index was not chosen or is unusable.
questions.hint: Seek or scan on index confirms usage.

questions.topic: A composite index and the order its columns have to be in
questions.learningObjective: Choose composite index column order
questions.stem: For queries filtering status then sorting created_at, which composite index order is best?

options.misconception: leading sort column prevents status seek

questions.explanation: Leading with the equality filter status allows a seek, and created_at second supports ordering. Reverse order cannot seek on status.

questions.topic: A covering index and the table visit it removes
questions.learningObjective: Design a covering index for a query
questions.stem: Design a covering index for SELECT name,status WHERE status='open' ORDER BY created_at.

answer.exemplar: Create an index on (status, created_at) INCLUDE (name) so filter, sort, and selected column are all served from the index.

questions.explanation: Include all filtered, sorted, and selected columns in the index. Then the engine avoids heap lookups entirely.
questions.hint: Index must include filter, sort, select.

questions.topic: A table scan in a plan and three ways to end it
questions.learningObjective: Fix a non-sargable predicate
questions.stem: WHERE LOWER(email)=LOWER('a@b.com') scans the table. Why?

options.misconception: case sensitivity is not the cause

options.text: LOWER is not a valid function
The function on the column prevents index use

questions.explanation: Applying a function to the indexed column makes the predicate non-sargable. Store a normalized column or use a functional index.

questions.topic: A cursor and an offset after a row above the page is deleted
questions.learningObjective: Prefer cursor pagination for stable lists
questions.stem: For a feed that changes often, which pagination is more stable?

options.misconception: offset shifts on inserts and deletes

options.text: Cursor based on a monotonic id

questions.explanation: Cursor pagination anchors on a value, so inserts and deletes above the page do not skip or duplicate rows. Offset is positional and fragile.

questions.topic: A cursor whose row is deleted before the next page is asked for
questions.learningObjective: Resume pagination after cursor row deletion
questions.stem: The cursor row is deleted; the next page request still sends last_id=42. What query should run?

options.misconception: looks for the deleted cursor row

questions.explanation: Use the cursor as an exclusive lower bound. The deleted row need not exist for the bound to work.
questions.hint: Cursor is a bound, not a row.

questions.topic: Overlapping pages and the duplicates an endless list has to drop
questions.learningObjective: Merge overlapping pages without duplicates
questions.stem: Pages overlap by one row due to a concurrent insert. How to render without duplicates?

options.text: Deduplicate by row id keeping first

options.misconception: may drop a legitimate new row

questions.explanation: Deduplicate by stable id during merge. This handles overlap caused by inserts or retries without losing data.

questions.topic: A rejected optimistic update and the newer edit a rollback discards
questions.learningObjective: Preserve server data after optimistic rejection
questions.stem: An optimistic update is rejected. The rollback also discards a newer server edit the client had not seen. What went wrong?

options.text: The client used PUT instead of PATCH

questions.explanation: Rolling back to a stale local snapshot can overwrite newer server data. Re-fetch or merge server state instead of restoring old local state.
questions.hint: Rollback to server state, not stale local.

questions.topic: A whole row write that overwrites a field nobody meant to change
questions.learningObjective: Avoid lost updates with partial writes
questions.stem: Why is PATCH safer than PUT for concurrent edits?

options.misconception: speed is not the safety benefit

questions.explanation: PATCH sends deltas, so fields updated by others are not clobbered. PUT replaces the whole resource and risks lost updates.

questions.topic: An offline queue and the retry policy that empties it
questions.learningObjective: Persist and drain an offline queue reliably
questions.stem: How should an offline queue be persisted and drained?

answer.exemplar: Persist the queue to durable storage, drain in insertion order with retries and backoff, and remove items only after server acknowledgement.

questions.explanation: Durable storage survives app restarts. Acknowledgement-based removal prevents data loss if a request fails mid-flight.

questions.topic: A message delivered three times and the consumer that applies it once
questions.learningObjective: Implement idempotent message handling
questions.stem: Design an idempotent consumer for at-least-once delivery.

answer.exemplar: Store processed message ids in a set; before handling, check and insert the id atomically, then apply the effect only if newly inserted.

questions.explanation: Atomic check-and-insert ensures duplicates are skipped even under concurrency. Use a transaction or unique constraint on the id.

questions.topic: A gap in a sequence and the messages that must wait for it
questions.learningObjective: Buffer out-of-order messages
questions.stem: Messages arrive as 1,3,2. What is the processing order?
questions.explanation: Buffer out-of-order messages and release them in sequence order once gaps fill. This preserves ordering guarantees.

questions.topic: A device that missed a delete and comes back with an old edit
questions.learningObjective: Reject stale edits against deleted items
questions.stem: A device pushes an edit for an item deleted on the server. What status should the server return?
questions.explanation: Return 404 or 410 to signal the resource is gone so the client can reconcile and remove it locally.

questions.topic: What a document shape permits that a table of columns cannot
questions.learningObjective: Choose document vs relational storage
questions.stem: When is a document store the better choice?

options.text: When data has a fixed schema and many joins
When strict ACID across tables is required
When records vary in shape and are read as a whole
When storage must be normalized to third normal form

questions.explanation: Documents suit variable shapes read as aggregates. Relational suits fixed schemas, joins, and strict consistency.

questions.topic: The write cost an index adds
questions.learningObjective: Balance index count against write throughput
questions.stem: A write-heavy table has twelve indexes. What is the likely problem?

options.misconception: fast reads are not a problem

options.text: Write throughput drops due to index maintenance

questions.explanation: Each index adds write amplification. Remove unused indexes and add only those serving measured queries.

questions.topic: Reading the three words a plan uses to describe its work
questions.learningObjective: Read a query plan's join strategy
questions.stem: Which plan node indicates a hash-based join?
questions.explanation: Hash Join builds a hash table on one input and probes with the other. Plan nodes name the strategy used.

questions.topic: A server-sent event and the one direction it allows
questions.learningObjective: Choose SSE vs WebSocket by directionality
questions.stem: For a one-way live feed from server to browser, which transport is simplest?
questions.explanation: SSE uses plain HTTP and auto-reconnects, making it simplest for one-way server-to-client streams. WebSockets fit bidirectional needs.
